prompt:
Write an essay of about 1,500 words on whether primary schools should still teach joined-up handwriting. Take a side and argue for it.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists.

text:
Primary schools should keep teaching joined-up handwriting. The case against it is not foolish, and it deserves a fair hearing, but it rests on a picture of what handwriting is for that is too narrow, and on an optimism about keyboards that the evidence does not support. Cursive, or whatever joined style a school adopts, is not a relic to be tidied away with the inkwell. It is a short, cheap, well-tested way of building fluency in a skill that children will use for the rest of their lives, and the time it takes is far smaller than its critics suggest.

Start with the strongest objection, which is that nobody writes by hand any more. This is an exaggeration, and a revealing one. Adults still write shopping lists, birthday cards, margin notes, forms, signatures and the quick reminder on the back of a hand. Pupils in secondary school and university still sit examinations by hand, and in most countries that is not about to change, because handwritten exams are cheap, secure and hard to cheat in. A child who cannot write quickly and legibly under time pressure is disadvantaged on the day it matters most. Fluent handwriting is therefore not a nostalgic extra but a gatekeeping skill, and the children who struggle with it are rarely the privileged ones who have a laptop and a tutor at home. Teaching it well in primary school is an equity measure. Dropping it leaves the children whose families cannot compensate to work it out alone.

The deeper objection is that typing is simply faster and cleaner, so why not teach that instead. But this presents a false choice. Nobody is proposing that children be kept away from keyboards; they should learn to type, and the sooner the better once their hands are big enough. The real question is whether handwriting should also be taught, and whether joined writing is the right form of it. On the first point, the research is fairly consistent that writing by hand does something that typing does not. Studies of young children learning letters have found that those who form letters by hand recognise them more reliably than those who type or trace them on a screen, probably because the movement of making a letter leaves a trace in memory that a keypress cannot. Brain imaging work, though still modest in scale and best treated with caution, points the same way: the motor and visual systems work together more when a child writes a letter than when they press a key. And studies of note-taking in older students, whatever the arguments about their size, suggest that longhand notes force the writer to compress and rephrase, where typing invites near-verbatim transcription. None of this proves that handwriting makes children cleverer. It does suggest that dropping it carries a cost that we have not properly priced.

That still leaves the narrower question of why joined-up writing, as opposed to print. Here the argument is practical rather than mystical. Print, with its lifted pen after every letter, is a fine starting point, and nobody should rush a five-year-old into loops and links before they can form single letters. But print has a ceiling. A child who writes entirely in separate letters tends to plateau at a speed that is adequate for a short sentence and frustrating for a page. Joining letters removes the pen lifts, builds rhythm, and lets the hand move across the line in a single flowing motion. Teachers who have taught both will tell you that the children who join early and confidently often write faster and with less fatigue, and that fatigue is not a trivial matter in a classroom where a pupil is asked to produce a paragraph about the Romans before lunch. When a child's hand aches after four lines, the content of those four lines suffers, because attention is being spent on the mechanics of writing rather than on what the child wants to say. Fluency frees up thought. That is the whole case for automatising any basic skill, from times tables to phonics, and handwriting belongs in the same family.

There is also a spelling argument that is easy to overlook. Joined writing treats a word as a unit, a single movement with a shape of its own. Children who write words in connected strokes build a kind of muscle memory for common letter patterns, such as the endings of words or the doubled letters that trip so many learners. Print encourages the child to think letter by letter, whereas joining encourages them to think in chunks, and chunking is how skilled spellers handle language. Some teachers of children with dyslexia, in particular, favour joined writing precisely because the continuous movement helps to prevent the reversal of letters such as b and d, which in print differ only by the side on which the bump sits. Again, the evidence here is not overwhelming and I would not claim more than it supports, but it points consistently in one direction and has no real counterpart on the other side.

The most common reply is that this is all very well, but the school day is crowded, and every minute spent on cursive is a minute taken from something else. This is where the argument is weakest, because the actual time involved is small. Handwriting is not a subject that needs an hour a day. Short, frequent, well-taught sessions of ten or fifteen minutes, spread across the early years, are what the best programmes use, and the skill is then exercised for free every time a child writes anything in any lesson. It is hard to think of another piece of the curriculum that is practised so often at so little additional cost. If we are looking for savings in a crowded timetable, a quarter of an hour of handwriting practice is a poor place to start, set against the volume of writing that follows from it.

The second reply is that joined writing is old-fashioned, and that many countries have moved away from it. Some have, and Finland made headlines when it replaced compulsory cursive with keyboard skills in its national curriculum. But the story is more mixed than the headline suggests. Several American states that dropped cursive from their standards after the Common Core reforms have since reintroduced it, and a number of European countries still teach a joined script. Where policy has swung back, it has done so in part because teachers reported that children could not read the handwritten comments they were given, could not read historical documents or a grandparent's letter, and could not produce a legible signature. A child who cannot read cursive is cut off from a large part of the written record, including family letters, old school registers and archival material. That is a quiet but real loss, and it is far easier to prevent than to repair.

A further point concerns the child's own sense of self. A person's handwriting is one of the few distinctive marks they carry, and learning to develop a personal hand is a small but real act of ownership. Children take visible pride in a page of tidy, flowing writing, and teachers know that the moment a pupil is first allowed to use a pen rather than a pencil is a small rite of passage. It would be a mistake to build a curriculum purely on such feelings, but it would equally be a mistake to dismiss them. Motivation matters in the early years, and a skill that children are proud of is a skill they are willing to practise.

None of this means the old way of teaching it should be defended wholesale. Too many children were once drilled in elaborate scripts, with looped capitals and fussy ascenders that nobody used in adult life, and were marked down for style rather than legibility. The sensible modern approach is to teach a simple, forward-sloping joined style with few decorations, introduce it once letter formation is secure, and prize legibility and speed over copperplate elegance. Children who find joining genuinely difficult, perhaps because of motor difficulties, should be supported to find a style that works for them rather than being forced into a uniform one. Flexibility of that kind is compatible with teaching joined writing to the great majority, and is better than abandoning it altogether.

It is fair to say that the evidence on cursive specifically, as opposed to handwriting in general, is thinner than its defenders sometimes claim. We do not have large trials showing that joined writing produces better outcomes than fluent print. But absence of proof is a weak reason for removing something that costs little, has plausible benefits, and is broadly trusted by the people who teach children to write for a living. The burden of proof should sit with those who want to change a long-standing practice, and so far they have offered an argument from convenience, which is not the same thing as an argument from learning.

Primary schools should therefore go on teaching joined-up handwriting, alongside keyboard skills rather than in competition with them. The case rests on fluency, on the demonstrated value of the hand in learning to write, on the continuing need to write by hand in examinations and daily life, on access to the written past, and on the small amount of time involved. A child who leaves primary school able to write a legible, comfortable, joined hand has gained a durable tool. A child who has not has lost something that is hard to recover later, and the cost falls hardest on those with the fewest alternatives at home. That is reason enough to keep the pen moving.
